questions.explanation: #19 puts the problem as community funds being used for something not everyone in the community agrees with, and #6 says public funds should not sponsor sex-work marketing while also saying no one else gets to decide how others use their money. The first option is the charge made in #1, which #6 and #12 deny, and the second contradicts #6. No one argued the last option.
options: Trans and Jewish people should not be welcome in the Zcash community, so a grant reaching them should end.
Sex workers should be prevented from using Zcash for their own payments, since their trade is considered immoral.
Community funds should not be spent sponsoring a controversial market that not everyone in the community supports.
ZCG should be shut down because it cannot be trusted to deal with hateful reactions to the grants it approves.
questions.prompt: Replying to emersonian, critics of the ZECsy grant stated their own objection. Which description fits it as they stated it (#6, #19)?

questions.explanation: #1 says debates about the grant and ZCG are healthy, and asks the community to call out attacks on identity loudly, even when they come from someone who agrees on the spending question. The second option is the caricature of the post that thowar2 objects to in #9, but #1 explicitly separates the two. Nothing in #1 asks for debate to stop.
options: Disagreeing with the grant, or wanting ZCG reformed or shut down, is healthy; attacking people for who they are should be called out, even from allies on spending.
Anyone who argues the ZECsy grant is a bad use of funds is spreading hate, and should be called out by name and shamed.
Debate about ZCG governance and the grant should stop until the community has finished tracking and eliminating hate in its ranks.
Hate matters only when it comes from critics of the grant, so supporters need not police the conduct of their own side.
questions.prompt: What line did emersonian actually draw in #1 between legitimate disagreement and hate?

questions.explanation: #11 replies that sex work is not a crime in many places and that US attitudes should not be Zcash's guiding values, and #17 adds that using private assets and listing privacy coins are illegal in some countries, asking who dictates illegality. Neither claimed that sex work is criminal everywhere, and no one argued that the approval settled the matter.
options: They said sex work is criminal everywhere but that criminality is irrelevant to the purposes of a privacy coin like Zcash.
They said the grant had already been approved by ZCG after review, so its marketing could no longer be revisited by anyone.
They said public marketing of any kind is a poor choice for Zcash and that the programme should simply be stopped altogether.
They said sex work is not a crime in many places, US attitudes should not guide Zcash, and illegality differs between countries anyway.
questions.prompt: Thowar2 said sex work is considered criminal and immoral in many places, making it a poor choice for public marketing (#6). How did others answer the point about criminality?

questions.explanation: #8 makes the darknet claim and nobody replies to it. The transphobia and antisemitism claim was met by requests for examples and denials in #2, #6 and #12. The funding point was answered in #17 and #21, and the illegal-activity point was met in #14 and #17.
options: That the reaction to the ZECsy booth photos included transphobia and antisemitism directed at members of the community.
That darknet markets sell drugs but not violence, CSAM, trafficking or sex work, as the author knows from having run one.
That public funds should not be used to sponsor marketing or conferences aimed at the sex-work and adult-content market.
That block reward subsidies and coin holder funds should not be used to promote illegal activities of any kind.
questions.prompt: Which of these points did no one in the thread respond to?

questions.explanation: #4 says it is happening on X, where practically nobody is standing up against hate, and #8 links one Bluesky post about how the community is coming across to an at-risk group. No quoted examples or usernames appear anywhere in the thread, which is why the request in #2 remains an open question.
options: Quoted forum posts from this thread containing transphobic and antisemitic remarks, with links to each of them.
A list of the usernames of participants in the forum who had made the remarks, together with links to their posts.
That it happens on X, where practically no one opposes it, plus a link to one Bluesky post about how the community comes across.
A refusal to give any, on the grounds that repeating the examples would only amplify them and harm the targets.
questions.prompt: Thailand85 asked for specific examples of the alleged hateful attacks (#2). What was offered in reply?

questions.explanation: #17 turns the standard back on itself by pointing out that illegality varies by country and that the grant itself pays for a legal booth for legal workers; #14 agrees with the principle and denies it applies. The second option borrows 'Code is amoral' from #8, which concerned how Zcash will be used, not what a grant may fund.
options: Who dictates illegality? Private assets and privacy coins are illegal in some countries; this grant pays for a legal booth marketing to legal workers.
Code is amoral, so a grant programme cannot be held responsible for anything its recipients later choose to do with the money.
Privacy matters more than any law, so a privacy project should fund any activity, whatever its legal status elsewhere.
ZCG screens every recipient for legal compliance in advance, so illegal activity could never be funded by the programme.
questions.prompt: Thailand85 said coin holder funds should not be used to promote illegal activity (#10, #16). Which is the strongest reply actually made?

questions.explanation: #6 says no one else gets to decide how others use their money but that using public funds to benefit one controversial market is irresponsible, and #19 repeats that the problem is community funds for something not everyone agrees with. The last option misreads #6, which separates this objection from any view of who should use Zcash.
options: Only members of mainstream, uncontroversial professions should be allowed to receive any grant-funded ZEC from the community.
People may use Zcash as they like, but that differs from the community paying to promote a controversial market many holders oppose.
Zcash should be marketed only to existing crypto users, who already understand privacy tools, exchanges and wallets.
Hostility toward sex workers is justified, because their trade is considered immoral and criminal in many places.
questions.prompt: Which is the strongest case actually made for objecting to the grant's marketing without hostility to the people involved?
